```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

mortensor builds probabilistic mortality forecasts from data observed at
different granularities. A forecast is assembled from interchangeable parts:

1. **data** in their original resolution (`mt_data()`),
2. **harmonisation** onto a modelling grid, single years of age by default
   (`mt_ungroup()`, `mt_smooth()`, `mt_regroup()`), bundled as a
   preprocessing pipeline (`mt_prep()`),
3. a **model** (`lee_carter()`, `rwd()`, `tucker3()`, `apc_bayes()`, ...),
   fitted with `mt_fit()` and forecast with `mt_forecast()` as simulated
   paths,
4. **evaluation** with rolling-origin backtests (`mt_backtest()`,
   `mt_score()`), and
5. **derived quantities** computed path by path (`life_expectancy()`).

This vignette uses simulated data with a known truth. The vignettes
"Data at different granularities" and "Forecasting with Human Mortality
Database data" apply the same steps to HMD data for England & Wales and
France.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
```

## Data

`mt_example()` simulates deaths for women and men aged 30 and over,
1990-2019. As in many official statistics, deaths are reported in 5-year age
groups with an open 90+ interval, exposures by single year of age with an
open 100+ interval.

```{r}
x <- mt_example()
x
mt_granularity(x)
```

`mt_validate()` checks plausibility (deaths without exposure, rates above 1,
coverage of the grid and, for stratified data, hierarchy sums):

```{r}
mt_validate(x)
```

## Harmonisation

The modelling grid is single years of age (30, ..., 99, 100+) and calendar
years. The deaths are coarser than the grid, so models cannot use them
directly:

```{r, error = TRUE}
mt_fit(lee_carter(), x)
```

`mt_ungroup()` estimates single-year deaths with the penalized composite link
model, using the single-year exposures as offset (deaths are ungrouped as
rates). The estimates add up to the observed group totals.

```{r}
u <- mt_ungroup(x)
head(attr(u, "ungroup"))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_ungroup(x, u, period = 2019)
```

Because the data are simulated, the estimated single-year rates can be
compared with the truth:

```{r}
est <- mt_array(u, "deaths") / mt_array(u, "exposure")
summary(as.vector(abs(log(est / attr(x, "truth")))))
```

## Fitting and forecasting

Preprocessing belongs to the model pipeline, so that backtests can refit it
on every training window:

```{r}
prep <- mt_prep(step_ungroup())
fit_lc <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), x, prep = prep)
fit_lc
fc_lc <- mt_forecast(fit_lc, h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
fc_lc
```

The forecast holds 500 simulated paths per age, year and stratum.
`mt_summarise()` returns means and quantiles:

```{r}
s <- mt_summarise(fc_lc)
s[age %in% c("65", "85") & period %in% c(2020, 2034), .(label, age, period, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_forecast(fc_lc, ages = c("40", "65", "85", "100+"))
```

## Derived quantities

Life expectancy is computed for every path, so its interval reflects the
joint uncertainty of all ages:

```{r}
e65 <- life_expectancy(fc_lc, at = 65)
e65[period %in% c(2020, 2027, 2034)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_life_expectancy(fc_lc, at = 65)
```

## Other models and ensembles

All models share the same interface. `tucker3()` models the strata jointly;
`mt_ensemble()` mixes the draws of several models.

```{r}
fit_t3 <- mt_fit(tucker3(), x, prep = prep)
ens <- mt_ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), t3 = tucker3(), rw = rwd())
fc_ens <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(ens, x, prep = prep), h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
life_expectancy(fc_ens, at = 65)[period == 2034]
```

## Honest backtests

`mt_backtest()` cuts the data at each forecast origin, refits the
preprocessing and the model on the training window, and scores predictive
draws against the observed deaths at their observed resolution (here 5-year
age groups), so ungrouping errors count against the model.

```{r}
origins <- 2004:2009
bt <- rbind(
  mt_backtest(lee_carter(), x, origins = origins, h = 10, prep = prep, n_draws = 200),
  mt_backtest(tucker3(), x, origins = origins, h = 10, prep = prep, n_draws = 200),
  mt_backtest(rwd(), x, origins = origins, h = 10, prep = prep, n_draws = 200)
)
mt_score(bt, by = "model")
```

Lower CRPS and WIS are better; `cov50`, `cov80` and `cov95` are the shares
of observations inside the central 50%, 80% and 95% intervals.

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_coverage(bt)
```
